title: Sedna (dwarf planet)
description: Distant body in the outer Solar System
wiki_lead:
Sedna (minor-planet number 90377) is a dwarf planet in the outermost reaches of the Solar System, orbiting the Sun far beyond the orbit of Neptune. It was discovered in 2003, and is roughly 1,000 km in diameter. Spectroscopic analysis has revealed its surface to be a mixture of the solid ices of water, carbon dioxide, and ethane, along with sedimentary deposits of methane-derived, reddish-colored tholins, a chemical makeup similar to the surfaces of other trans-Neptunian objects. Sedna is not expected to have a substantial atmosphere. Within the range of uncertainty, it is tied with Ceres in the asteroid belt as the largest dwarf planet not known to have a moon. Owing to its lack of known moons, Sedna's mass and density remain unknown.
Sedna takes approximately 11,400 years to complete one orbit around the Sun. Its orbit is one of the widest known in the Solar System. Its aphelion is located 937 astronomical units (AU) away, about 19 times farther than that of Pluto. Sedna's orbit is also one of the most elliptical discovered, with an eccentricity of 0.85. As of 2026, Sedna is 83.0 AU (12.4 billion km) from the Sun, 2.5 times as far away as Neptune.
Upon its discovery, Sedna was initially classified as a member of the scattered disc, a group of objects sent into high-eccentricity orbits by the gravitational influence of Neptune. Some astronomers instead referred to it as the first known member of the inner Oort cloud, as its perihelion at 76.2 AU (11.4 billion km) is far too distant for it to have been scattered by any of the known planets. It has since become the prototype of a new class of objects characterized by highly eccentric orbits with very distant perihelia, the sednoids. The astronomer Michael E. Brown, co-discoverer of Sedna, has argued that its unusual orbit could provide information on the early evolution of the Solar System. Sedna might have been perturbed into its orbit through a close gravitational encounter with the hypothetical Planet Nine.

History


Discovery
Sedna (provisionally designated 2003 VB12) was discovered by Michael Brown (Caltech), Chad Trujillo (Gemini Observatory), and David Rabinowitz (Yale University) on 14 November 2003. The discovery formed part of a survey begun in 2001 with the Samuel Oschin telescope at Palomar Observatory near San Diego, California, using Yale's 160-megapixel Palomar Quest camera. On that day, an object was observed to move by 4.6 arcseconds over 3.1 hours relative to stars, which indicated that its distance was about 100 AU. Follow-up observations were made in November–December 2003 with the SMARTS (Small and Medium Research Telescope System) at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile, the Tenagra IV telescope in Nogales, Arizona, and the Keck Observatory on Mauna Kea in Hawaii. grok_lead: Sedna, officially designated (90377) Sedna, is a large trans-Neptunian object and dwarf planet candidate in the outermost reaches of the Solar System. Discovered on November 14, 2003, by Michael E. Brown, Chadwick Trujillo, and David Rabinowitz using the Samuel Oschin Telescope at Palomar Observatory, Sedna is distinguished by its extremely detached, highly elliptical orbit, with a perihelion distance of approximately 76 AUâthe highest known perihelion among large trans-Neptunian objects of comparable sizeâand an orbital period of roughly 11,000â12,000 years. This makes Sedna one of the most distant and isolated known objects orbiting the Sun, far beyond the Kuiper belt and potentially part of an inner Oort cloud population. Named after the Inuit goddess of the sea and marine animals due to its frigid, remote location, Sedna's orbit is so elongated that it approaches the Sun only once every several millennia, with aphelion extending nearly 1,000 AU. Sedna's discovery was announced in March 2004 and marked a significant finding as the most distant object known in the Solar System at the time, located about 8 billion miles (13 billion kilometers) from Earthâthree times farther from Earth than Pluto at the time. Its extreme orbit suggests it may have been perturbed by gravitational influences such as passing stars or unseen distant bodies early in the Solar System's history, providing clues about the formation and dynamics of the outer Solar System. Observations indicate Sedna is reddish in colorâamong the reddest objects in the Solar System after Marsâand likely consists of a mixture of ices and organic compounds, though its surface composition remains not fully understood and differs from typical Kuiper belt objects. Estimates of Sedna's size place it at roughly 900â1,200 km in diameter, making it comparable to some recognized dwarf planets, though it has not been officially classified as such by the International Astronomical Union. Its surface temperature is estimated to never rise above about â240 Â°C (â400 Â°F), and Hubble Space Telescope observations have ruled out the presence of a large moon, despite earlier hints from its slow rotation period. Sedna's ongoing perihelion approach (expected around 2075â2076) will allow brighter observations in coming decades, potentially revealing more about its properties.
